54	## 畫面：中文與 KK 音標
55	
56	FM-1 的字型只有 ASCII，KK 音標的 `ə ɪ æ θ ð ʃ ŋ` 也不在裡面。
57	
58	- **只把 deck 用到的字做成 subset 字型**：用 [Cubic 11](https://github.com/ACh-K/Cubic-11)（繁體中文 11×11 點陣，OFL-1.1）。2,500 個字 1-bit 約 40 KB，KK 符號另外幾十個。
59	- 卡片文字存成 glyph 編號（中文 2 B 一字），由電腦在匯入時決定。
60	- Conductor 的做法（電腦把每行畫成 240×16 的點陣，549 B 一行）適合連線即時顯示，不適合離線存幾千張卡。
61	
62	## flash 預算（3,000 字）
63	
64	| 項目 | 大小 |
65	|---|---|
66	| app 程式 + 字型（Morse 0.3 約 128 KB） | 約 130 KB |
67	| Klatt 合成器 | 幾十 KiB |
68	| 單字 + 音素 + 中文釋義（glyph 編號），不含例句 | 約 120 KB |
69	| 加上例句與例句翻譯 | 約 300 KB |
70	| 中文 subset 字型 | 約 40 KB |
71	| FSRS 狀態 | 約 24 KB（存在資料區，A/B 兩份） |
72	
73	不含例句的版本可以整個編進 581,564 B 的韌體槽；含例句就需要下面的「資料區」或壓縮（fm1-base 有 `tools/lz4blk.py`）。
74	
75	## 字卡怎麼進機器 {#delivery}
76	
77	1. **v1：編進韌體映像。** 換 deck = 重新 build + 刷寫，每次都要本人同意；只寫韌體區（和 Morse 升級一樣），不碰 SLOOP 的資料，完全符合現有的安全規則。
78	2. **選用：app 自己寫 flash 資料區。** 用 USB 隨時推送新 deck，不必重刷。這條路**要先修改 AGENTS.md** 的「不直接 erase/program」規則，等真的要做時再請本人核准。規則草稿：
79	    - 只能用 fm1-base 的 `plat_data_erase` / `plat_data_write`（有 `PLAT_DATA_OK` 邊界檢查），不能自己算位址以外的範圍。
80	    - deck 區是 app.h 裡宣告的固定 sector 範圍，必須是最新備份裡確認為空、且不和 SLOOP 的 project / sample、Morse 的 `0xDA000` 重疊的 sector。
81	    - 改 deck 區之前先跑 `just emu-rehearse`，並更新 [flash 配置圖](../hardware/flash-map.md)。
82	    - 寫入的資料先算 CRC，寫完讀回比對，失敗就當作沒有 deck。
83	3. **只在連線時串流**：電腦即時送卡片，排程直接用 Anki 的。完全不寫 flash，但離開電腦就不能用；可以當作第一個試做版。
84	
85	fm1-base 的 resource region（`resources = FILE`）不適合拿來放可替換的 deck：build 會把資料的長度與 CRC 編進韌體，換資料仍然要重 build。
86	
87	## Roadmap
88	
89	1. 語音方案定案（聽完 `just voice-open` 的試聽頁）。如果選 Klatt，要先把 Moonshine 的 C++ 移植成 C（fm1-base 的 app 是 C）。
90	2. 電腦端：Anki `.apkg` reader、NGSL + ECDICT + OpenCC 的內建字表產生器、subset 字型產生器、FSRS 參考數據。
91	3. 韌體 v1：開機卡片、四鍵評分、選擇題、拼字、遺忘曲線、FSRS，deck 編進映像。
92	4. 同步：日期、複習紀錄、AnkiConnect 寫回。
93	5. 之後如果要上 Firmware Hub，比照 Morse 拆成獨立 repo 再掛成 submodule（見 [Hub](../firmware/hub.md)）。
94

````text
1	# 自製韌體環境
2	
3	目標是把 **改 code → host simulator → fm1-emu → 批准 → 實機** 整條鏈跑通，再談功能。基礎是 [fm1-base](https://github.com/charlesvestal/fm1-base)（MPL-2.0，beta）：它在 felucca-bsp 之上提供螢幕、按鍵、LED、音訊、MIDI、storage，以及跑同一份 app 的 host simulator。
4	
5	**狀態（2026-11-18）：host simulator、實機套件 build、fm1-emu 兩種晶片開機都已跑通；自己的 build 已經刷進實機過（Conductor 0.1、0.2，Morse 0.1–0.3，紀錄見[我的機器](../device-log.md)）。**
6	
7	## 結構
8	
9	```text
10	third_party/fm1-base/      git submodule（它自己再帶 felucca-bsp 於 bsp/）
11	firmware/hello/            fm1-base template 的原樣複本，用來驗證整條鏈
12	firmware/conductor/        agent 控制台（見 Conductor 頁）
13	firmware/morse/            摩斯電碼機（見摩斯電碼機頁）
14	firmware/common/           app 之間共用的模組（hostlink、ledfx、chime、lpc、adpcm）
15	firmware/voicelab/         語音解碼器的驗證 app（見裝置端語音合成頁；不刷實機）
16	firmware/<app>/            之後的 app
17	tools/jieli/               JieLi toolchain（gitignore）
18	tools/fw-AC79_AIoT_SDK/    JieLi AC79 SDK，固定 tag（gitignore）
19	```
20	
21	這符合上游的建議：把 `template/` 複製到自己的 repo，fm1-base 放在旁邊當 submodule。`tools/build.py APP_DIR` 接受任意位置的 app 目錄。
22	
23	## 指令
24	
25	| 指令 | 作用 | 我跑過嗎 |
26	|---|---|---|
27	| `just fw-setup` | 初始化 submodule、安裝 Python 工具（`fw` dependency group） | 是 |
28	| `just fw-test [app]` | build host simulator 並跑 `tests/basic.txt`，產出截圖與 WAV 到 `firmware/<app>/build/host/` | 是，全部 `ok` |
29	| `just fw-toolchain` | 下載 JieLi toolchain 與 AC79 SDK 到 `tools/`（約 1.2 GB） | 是 |
30	| `just fw-build [app]` | build 實機套件 `firmware/<app>/build/*.fwsc` | 是，約 17 秒，產出 `template.fwsc`（616 KB，identity `FM-1_1100`） |
31	
32	## 前置需求（macOS）
33	
34	- `uv`、`just`、Xcode command line tools（`cc`）。
35	- **`brew install libraqm`。** fm1-base 的字型產生器（`tools/gen_font.py`）用到 OpenType features，需要 Pillow 帶 libraqm。macOS 的 Pillow wheel 編譯時沒有包含它（`HAVE_RAQM = False`），所以 `pyproject.toml` 設了 `no-binary-package = ["pillow"]`，讓 Pillow 從原始碼對 Homebrew 的 libraqm 編譯。沒裝的話 `gen_font.py` 會報 `not supported without libraqm`。`[實機]` host 端
36	- 實機 build 另外需要 **Docker**：JieLi toolchain 只有 Linux x86-64，`build.py` 在 macOS 上會自動把每個工具放進 `linux/amd64` 容器執行。
37	
38	## 兩段式 build
39	
40	| | Host simulator | 實機套件 |
41	|---|---|---|
42	| 指令 | `build.py APP --host` | `build.py APP` |
43	| 需要 | 本機 C 編譯器 | JieLi toolchain + AC79 SDK + Docker |
44	| 產出 | `build/host/<name>_host` | `build/<name>.fwsc` |
45	| 用途 | 日常迭代、邏輯與畫面測試 | 模擬器與實機 |
46	
47	Host simulator 讀一份腳本（`tests/basic.txt`）注入按鍵與 MIDI、檢查狀態、存截圖與音訊。這是讓 agent 自己驗證改動的主要手段，不需要任何硬體。
48	
49	## Build 結果
50	
51	`just fw-build hello` 的輸出（2026-11-17）：app 226,264 B；RAM code 9,296 / 32,768 B；`.data+.bss` 76,452 / 98,304 B；build 自帶的檢查全部 `ok`（沒有 soft-double、register 存取只在 felucca-bsp 內）。
52	
53	在 fm1-emu 開機 `[模擬]`：
54	
55	| 晶片 | 結果 |
56	|---|---|
57	| `uc25hq80` | 開機到 TEMPLATE 畫面，5 秒內 12 次 flash erase / program |
58	| `p25q80` | 同上，12 次 |
59	
60	兩種晶片行為一致。這只是開機與寫入次數，「改設定 → 重開 → 讀回」還沒做。
61	
62	!!! note "之前卡住的地方"
63	    第一次 build 失敗是因為 Docker daemon 的 proxy 連不上，拉不到 `debian:bookworm-slim`（`build: cannot start the toolchain container`）。修好 Docker 的網路後就正常。遇到同樣訊息先查 `docker pull --platform linux/amd64 debian:bookworm-slim` 能不能成功。
64	
65	## 預設的 template 帶 Bluetooth
66	
67	`firmware/hello/fm1.toml` 是 `ble = true`，會用到 SDK 裡 JieLi 的 Bluetooth library（binary only）。如果第一次 build 想降低變數，可以加 `--no-ble`（產出 `NAME-usb.fwsc`）。
68	
69	## Release 與另開 repo 的問題
70	
71	fm1-base template 附的 release workflow（透過共用的 [zvenson/fm1-build](https://github.com/zvenson/fm1-build) 產生 build attestation，Firmware Hub 才會標 built from source）假設的是**獨立的 firmware repo**：app 在 `app/`、fm1-base 在 `base/`、根目錄有 `./build.sh`。放在這個筆記 repo 的子目錄不符合那個配置，所以我把複本裡的 `.github/` 拿掉了。
72	
73	結論：在本機迭代、刷自己的機器，子目錄就夠。**等某個 app 要正式 release 時，再把它搬到獨立 repo，並以 submodule 引回這裡。**
74	
75	## 自製韌體的規則
76	
77	寫在 `AGENTS.md`，重點：
78	
79	1. 先 `just fw-test`，再用 `just emu-run` 在**兩種晶片**各跑一次，才提實刷。
80	2. 存檔只走 fm1-base 的 storage 層，它處理新舊晶片的 JEDEC ID。不自己寫 flash 位址。
81	3. 自製韌體每一次實刷都要我批准，和裝別人的韌體一樣。
82	4. build 產物不進 git。
83	
84	## 下一步
85	
86	- [x] 跑通 `just fw-build hello`
87	- [x] `just emu-shot firmware/hello/build/template.fwsc` 兩種晶片都開機
88	- [ ] `just emu-run firmware/hello/build/template.fwsc` 兩種晶片各一次，改設定、重開、確認保存
89	- [ ] 批准後刷進實機，按鍵 → USB MIDI → host 端 `mido` 腳本收得到
90	- [ ] 開第一個自己的 app：最小的 MIDI controller / macro pad（按鍵送 MIDI、螢幕顯示 layer）
91	- [x] 依 [Agent Deck 試用](../firmware/agent-deck/index.md)的心得，決定 agent 控制台是 fork Agent Deck 還是在 fm1-base 上重寫：**在 fm1-base 上重寫**，見 [Conductor](../agentic/conductor.md)（`firmware/conductor`，共用模組在 `firmware/common`）
92

The search turned up several sources on the progression, which is called 王道進行 (Ōdō shinkō) in Japanese.

- **Basic form:** The English Wikipedia article describes the pop version as IV–V–iii–vi, which drops the seventh notes, and says an ii–V–I cadence can extend it. (Wikipedia, "Royal road progression")
- **Japanese naming:** A Wikipedia article on the IV△7–V7–iii7–vi version gives 王道進行 and 小悪魔コード進行 (Koakuma) as alternate names, and notes it is common in contemporary Japanese pop. (Wikipedia mirror, IV△7–V7–iii7–vi progression)
- **Origin:** A Japanese-language source credits Tetsuya Komuro's vi–IV–V–I "Komuro progression" as a related pattern. The article also traces the earliest J-pop use to Yumi Arai's 1974 song "Yasashisa ni Tsutsumareta Nara," with a complete version appearing after a lowered note in Hi-Fi Set's 1975 hit "Sotsugyou Shashin." (Kiwix Wikipedia mirror, Royal road progression)
- **Prevalence:** One mirror says that, as of 2023, about 40% of Japan's top twenty best-selling singles of all time use the progression. (Kiwix Wikipedia mirror)
- **Example in F:** A guitar-chord site gives F–G–Em–Am (with seventh chords FMaj7–G7–Em7–Am7) as the standard example, and lists songs such as LiSA's "Gurenge" and TK's "Unravel" among uses. (guitarcomposerstoolbox.com, C and D pages)

The sources differ on details. The English Wikipedia article is the most current version I found, but the older mirrors include slightly different examples and citations, and some guitar-site claims are not backed by a published source.

The search turned up the study's bibliographic details and a summary of its main finding, though not the full text.

- **Citation:** Duke, Simmons & Cash (2009), "It's Not How Much; It's How: Characteristics of Practice Behavior and Retention of Performance Skills," *Journal of Research in Music Education*, 56(4), 310-321. The authors were affiliated with the University of Texas at Austin, the University of Texas at San Antonio, and Texas Tech University.
- **Participants:** The sample was 17 graduate and advanced-undergraduate piano majors in performance and pedagogy programs at the Sarah and Ernest Butler School of Music at The University of Texas at Austin.
- **Main finding:** Total practice time and the number of repetitions did not predict how well students played a passage the next day. What mattered was locating the specific hard section and repeating it until it was fixed (pinpointing and repeating the exact hard bit until it was fixed).
- **Limitations:** One summary notes the study is correlational, not experimental, so it cannot prove the strategies caused the better performance. It also involved a single short passage.

A caution: a learn-log.pages.dev page attributes a specific tempo recommendation to this study (isolating sections and building tempo gradually, starting at 50% of target). I could not confirm that in any of the sources returned, so I would not rely on that attribution without checking the original paper.

```text
1	# fm1-base
2	
3	A base for M-VAVE FM-1 firmware, on [felucca-bsp](https://github.com/hugelton/felucca-bsp): the platform layer
4	above the hardware (screen, drawing and fonts, panel, LEDs, audio, MIDI over USB and TRS, storage, the screen reader),
5	a host simulator and a browser emulator that run the same app, and the tools to build, package and install it.
6	MPL-2.0: an app built on it may use any licence. See [DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md), [LICENSING.md](LICENSING.md) and
7	[CREDITS.md](CREDITS.md).
8	
9	**Status: beta.** Two firmwares are built on it so far, and they are its proof points:
10	[CTL-1](https://github.com/charlesvestal/fm1-ctl) (with Bluetooth MIDI) and
11	[Radio](https://github.com/charlesvestal/fm1-radio) (with WiFi). Expect the platform interface (`include/plat.h`)
12	and `fm1.toml`'s settings to change before 1.0.
13	
14	The template (`template/`) runs on an FM-1: screen, keys and their LEDs, sound, MASTER, encoders, settings kept
15	across a power cycle, USB-MIDI both ways, the screen reader, and an update started from the template itself. The same
16	app runs on the computer in the host simulator and in the browser: try the template's at
17	<https://charlesvestal.github.io/fm1-base/emu/>.
18	
19	    git clone --recursive https://github.com/charlesvestal/fm1-base
20	
21	## Optional parts
22	
23	A firmware has only what its fm1.toml asks for (and its app.h, for velocity and pressure); every build prints the
24	parts it has.
25	
26	| Part | How to include it | What the app calls |
27	| --- | --- | --- |
28	| Bluetooth MIDI with a computer or tablet | `ble = true` (`tools/build.py --no-ble` leaves it out of one build) | `TO_BLE`, `PORT_BLE`; `plat_ble_state`, `plat_ble_connected`; `plat_ble_enable`; with `ble_stack = "own"` a stream of SysEx frames read by the radio at the link's rate (`plat_ble_stream`: a screen mirrored) and the link as agreed (`plat_ble_link_info`) |
29	| Bluetooth MIDI devices (the FM-1 connects to a keyboard or controller) | `ble_central = true`, with `ble` | `plat_ble_scan`, `plat_ble_found`, `plat_ble_connect`, `plat_ble_disconnect`, `plat_ble_device`; `TO_BLE_HOST`, `TO_BLE_DEV`, `plat_midi_in_from` (one link at a time); `plat_ble_passkey` on the own stack |
30	| Bluetooth on fm1-base's own stack instead of JieLi's libraries (below) | `ble_stack = "own"`, with `ble` | the same calls |
31	| Pairing on the own stack (LE legacy pairing, the bond kept) | `ble_pairing = true`, with `ble_stack = "own"` | nothing |
32	| Bluetooth MIDI in by the sender's time (for an app that follows a clock by time) | `ble_midi_time = true`, with `ble_stack = "own"` | `plat_midi_in_t24` after `plat_midi_in` |
33	| Bluetooth audio to headphones and speakers (A2DP) | `bt_audio = true`, with `ble_stack = "own"`; `bt_log = true` puts its set-up on the radio's log | `plat_bta_on`, `plat_bta_scan`, `plat_bta_found`, `plat_bta_known`, `plat_bta_pick`, `plat_bta_reconnect`, `plat_bta_forget`, `plat_bta_hangup`, `plat_bta_state` |
34	| USB audio: the FM-1 recorded over the cable | on unless `usb_audio_in = false` | nothing: the app's output at MASTER, without the computer's audio (taken before it is mixed in) |
35	| USB audio: a computer plays through the FM-1 | on unless `usb_audio_out = false` (needs the input too) | nothing: mixed after the app and after the recording's tap, at MASTER; `plat_usb_play_gain` (0 muted .. 4096, the default) for the app's own setting |
36	| USB MIDI after the USB audio interfaces, so macOS 13-15 show the audio device | on with the USB audio input, unless `usb_midi_last = false` | nothing |
37	| Velocity and pressure from the keys | `#define APP_TOUCH` in app.h | `touch_on`, `touch_poll`, `touch_keys`, `touch_vel`, `touch_pressure` (lib/touch.h) |
38	| WiFi: a station on the networks around, with lwIP's sockets | `wifi = true` (not with `ble`, yet), and `net = [...]` for the app's network code | `plat_wifi_on`, `plat_wifi_state`, `plat_wifi_scan`, `plat_wifi_found`, `plat_wifi_join`, `plat_wifi_saved`, `plat_wifi_forget`, `plat_net_task` |

40	| USB audio at full level, MASTER for the speaker and headphones only | with the USB audio input | `plat_usb_audio_full` (the app's setting) |
41	| Screen mirroring: the screen and panel live on a computer (web/mirror, a PNG with `tools/fm1_mirror.py`), the panel played from it | `mirror = true` | nothing; `APP_REDRAW` (what a slow link dropped, drawn again), `APP_MIRROR_TEST` (a test session from the remote) |
42	| Backup and restore of the app's saved objects over USB, all or nothing (web/backup, `tools/fm1_backup.py`) | `backup = true` | app.h: `APP_BACKUP_OBJS`, `APP_BACKUP_MAGIC`, `APP_BACKUP_VERSION`, `APP_BACKUP_WHAT`; `app_backup_playing`, `_flush`, `_hold`, `_restored` |

44	| The USB host's device by name (its product string), for the app's own page | `#define APP_USB_HOST_NAME` in app.h, with `usb_host` | `plat_usb_host_name` |
45	| The second core: a worker for part of the render (how to use it: [docs/SECOND-CORE.md](docs/SECOND-CORE.md)) | `cpu2 = true`; `cpu2_fallback = true` for one core after a failure instead of a restart; `cpu2_stack` | `plat_cpu2_set(1)` in `app_init`; `plat_cpu2_run`, `plat_cpu2_wait` in the render; `plat_cpu2_sync`, `plat_core`; `plat_cpu2_gave_up`, `plat_cpu2_barred` |
46	| Lower case in the big fonts | `font_full = ["L"]` | the fonts as ever |
47	| The firmware as an `.rfm1` for host apps (RemoteFM1 for iOS), below | `tools/build.py APP_DIR --rfm1` | nothing |
48	| The browser emulator's own parts (`tools/build.py --web`): web/emu/parts, each file saying what it does; without any, the page and app.wasm are as before. One is on without asking: `resample`, the FM-1's 44.1 kHz played at the browser's rate (many computers run audio at 48 kHz), where the page takes parts (fm1-base's page and worklet) | `emu = ["name", ...]`, `"-resample"` to leave it out (or `FM1B_EMU="name ..."` for one build: those parts only) | nothing, unless a part says so |
49	
50	Every firmware also counts each port's MIDI messages, in and out: `plat_midi_count(PORT_*, out)` for counters,
51	`plat_midi_ago` for activity lights.
52	And: `plat_midi_out_room(to)` (room in the out queues, each Bluetooth link's its own, for a sequencer's note-offs),
53	`plat_midi_in_from()` (where the last message in came from, as an out: for MIDI thru) and `plat_midi_out_link()` (a new
54	USB connection); `plat_store_size` and `plat_store_head` (an object whole or not at all; its header only); big data in
55	flash beyond the store with `plat_data*`, in the data area and two more windows (`PLAT_XDATA0`, `PLAT_XDATA1`), and a
56	third on request (`xdata2 = true`: `PLAT_XDATA2`, 0xFC000..0xFEFFF).
57	
58	## Bluetooth and WiFi
59	
60	A firmware has Bluetooth or WiFi, not both: each fills most of what the FM-1 has (the chip has no external RAM),
61	and together they don't fit. WiFi, and Bluetooth on JieLi's stack, need JieLi's AC79 SDK (`$AC79_SDK`) for its
62	libraries. Bluetooth on fm1-base's own stack (`ble_stack = "own"`) links nothing of JieLi's, and neither does a
63	build without a radio. Every build still takes the three SDK files a package needs (LICENSING.md).
64	
65	### Two Bluetooth stacks
66	
67	By default (`ble = true`), Bluetooth runs on JieLi's binary libraries from the SDK, through a shim (`ble/`). With
68	`ble_stack = "own"` it runs instead on Henri David's stack from [Optimist](https://github.com/w0ts/optimist),
69	in `bt/` under MPL-2.0, with felucca-bsp's radio drivers. Nothing of JieLi's is linked, there is no shim and no
70	task, and the build checks it. The radio calibrates itself at every start, so an FM-1 whose stock calibration was
71	overwritten works the same. The own stack is smaller and does more:
72	
73	- Bluetooth MIDI with a computer or a phone, as on JieLi's.
74	- With `ble_pairing = true` it pairs and encrypts the link (LE legacy pairing), and keeps the bond in `OBJ_BLE`.
75	  Without it a pairing is refused; macOS and iOS connect anyway.
76	- `ble_diag = false` leaves out the link layer's diagnostics (its counters and event rings: about 2.4 KB of RAM
77	  and some code; the radio log's `BT ll` line). They are kept by default.
78	- With `ble_midi_time = true` each message from Bluetooth comes with the time it was sent, from its BLE-MIDI
79	  timestamp (`plat_midi_in_t24`): the connection's bunching taken out, for an app that times a clock it follows
80	  itself. Without it the clock and transport are held to the sender's time (spaced as sent, up to 0.12 s later).
81	- With `ble_central = true` the FM-1 connects to Bluetooth MIDI devices, as on JieLi's. A device that asks for a
82	  code gets one on the FM-1's screen (`plat_ble_passkey`).
83	- With `bt_audio = true` it sends its sound to headphones and speakers (A2DP, SBC), beside Bluetooth MIDI on the
84	  one radio. While it streams, the FM-1's own output is muted. Four devices are remembered, the last one first, and
85	  `plat_bta_reconnect(0)` at power-on connects it again. `bt_log = true` adds the audio set-up's steps to the
86	  radio's log.
87	
88	It was tried on one FM-1 with a Mac, an iPhone (GarageBand; Cubasis as host and as a peripheral with the code),
89	headphones (AIAIAI TMA-2) and a speaker (Anker SoundCore 2), MIDI and audio at once. Its limits:
90	
91	- One Bluetooth MIDI link at a time: while the FM-1 is connected to a device, a computer can't connect to it
92	  (JieLi's keeps both).
93	- Audio reaches the ear 150-300 ms after a key (the device's own buffer): for listening, not for playing in time.
94	- After an abrupt drop, a speaker may not answer for a minute or two.
95	- Each firmware keeps its own keys. After switching firmware, forget the FM-1 on the phone or speaker and pair
96	  again.
97	
98	`examples/ble_own` is the template on the own stack with every option. For how the stack works, see
99	[docs/bt/README.md](docs/bt/README.md).
100	
101	### Turning Bluetooth on
102	
103	1. In fm1.toml, `ble = true`. Add `ble_central = true` for the FM-1 to connect to MIDI devices too (a keyboard,
104	   a controller), beside a computer. For the own stack, add `ble_stack = "own"` and its options (above).
105	2. In app.h, give it a store object: `OBJ_BLE` in the app's object enum, and its offset in `APP_STORE_MAP` (the
106	   radio's address and pairing are kept there). On the own stack an app may keep them in its own saved data instead
107	   (a settings record of its own): `#define APP_BLE_STORE` and `app_ble_load` / `app_ble_save` (plat.h `struct
108	   plat_ble_rec`), and no `OBJ_BLE`.
109	3. In the app: MIDI goes out with `TO_BLE` and comes in on `PORT_BLE`, as USB's does. For a page of devices, add
110	   `#define APP_BTDEV` to app.h and use lib/btdev.h (the template's REC does).
111	4. With devices there are two links, the computer's and the device's. `TO_BLE` goes to both; `TO_BLE_HOST` or
112	   `TO_BLE_DEV` goes to one, each with its own queue, so a slow device never holds up the computer. Both come in on
113	   `PORT_BLE`, and `plat_midi_in_from()` says which. MIDI thru, with nothing sent back where it came from (a keyboard
114	   played through to a phone): after each `plat_midi_in`,
115	   `plat_midi_send(pkt, (TO_USB | TO_BLE) & ~plat_midi_in_from())`.
116	
117	Bluetooth starts at every power-on, as on M-VAVE's firmware, unless the last Bluetooth run crashed. A firmware
118	that lets the player turn it off keeps that as a setting, calls `plat_ble_enable(0)` / `plat_ble_enable(1)` when it
119	changes, and tells the platform whether to start it at power-on with `APP_BLE_AT_BOOT` in app.h (an expression,
120	e.g. `(set.bluetooth != 0)`). Off ends every link and stops advertising and scanning: the radio is quiet. Its manual
121	should say where the setting is (the template's: for details, see template/docs/MANUAL.md).
122	`tools/build.py --no-ble` builds the same firmware without Bluetooth (NAME-usb.fwsc).
123	
124	### Turning WiFi on
125	
126	1. In fm1.toml, `wifi = true` (and not `ble`). Leave USB audio out (`usb_audio_in = false`, `usb_audio_out =
127	   false`): WiFi needs its RAM.
128	2. In app.h, two store objects: `OBJ_BLE` (the radio's address and calibration) and `OBJ_WIFI` (the networks
129	   kept), with their offsets in `APP_STORE_MAP`; and a smaller canvas, `#define APP_CANVAS_PX (240u * 48u)` (draw
130	   the screen in strips 48 rows high or less).
131	3. The app's network code goes in its own files, listed in fm1.toml's `net = [...]`: they're built as the SDK
132	   builds code that talks lwIP, and include `lwip/sockets.h`. That code runs in a task of its own
133	   (`plat_net_task`): a socket call waits, and the main loop must not.
134	4. In the app: `plat_wifi_on(1)` turns it on; it joins the networks it joined before (six, the most recent first).
135	   `plat_wifi_scan` and `plat_wifi_found` list the networks around, `plat_wifi_join` joins one (kept once joined),
136	   `plat_wifi_state` and `plat_wifi_ip` say how far it got. Passwords come over USB:
137	   `tools/fm1_remote.py wifi join SSID PASSWORD` (or typed on the keys: Radio has a page for it).
138	
139	For a working example, see `examples/wifi`; for a whole firmware, fm1-radio.
140	
141	### What each costs
142	
143	The FM-1 has a 581 KB app slot in the flash, 96 KB of RAM for `.data` and `.bss` (128 KB in a WiFi build), and a
144	336 KB pool of RAM for big buffers (304 KB in a WiFi build). With `ram_layout = "packed"` in fm1.toml
145	(`device/app_packed.ld`) the RAM code, `.data` and `.bss` and the pool share one budget of 464 KB instead, packed from
146	its bottom, 8 KB kept spare (and `main_stack` / `irq_stack` may give it the stacks' unused part). Measured on the
147	template (October 2026), in KB:
148	
149	| | Flash | RAM | Pool |
150	| --- | --- | --- | --- |
151	| The template without a radio (`--no-ble`) | 77 | 27 | 68 |
152	| Bluetooth MIDI with a computer (`ble`) | + 124 | + 45 | + 24 |
153	| Bluetooth MIDI devices too (`ble_central`) | + 8 | + 1 | 0 |
154	| Bluetooth MIDI with a computer on the own stack (`ble_stack = "own"`) | + 41 to 46 | + 10 | + 1 |
155	| Pairing, devices and Bluetooth audio too (`ble_pairing`, `ble_central`, `bt_audio`) | + 57 to 62 | + 8 | + 30 |
156	| WiFi (`wifi`, from fm1-radio's measurements) | + about 300 | + about 100 | + about 276 |
157	
158	- Bluetooth: JieLi's BT controller and stack (the flash), its 24 KB heap and their tables (the RAM), three task
159	  stacks of 8 KB (the pool). The template with Bluetooth and devices is 214 KB of flash, 75 of 96 KB of RAM: room
160	  for a big app (CTL-1, with a General MIDI synth, is 491 KB).
161	- The own stack: the template with Bluetooth MIDI alone is 118 to 123 KB of flash, 37 KB of RAM and 69 KB of pool;
162	  with pairing, devices and audio, 180 KB, 45 KB and 99 KB. On a big app the
163	  difference shows: LOOM-8 on JieLi's stack is 506 KB of flash, 88 KB of RAM and 327 KB of pool; on the own stack
164	  with MIDI alone, 454 KB, 68 KB and 318 KB; with pairing, devices, audio and its pages for them, 512 KB, 91 KB and
165	  328 KB.
166	- WiFi: JieLi's driver (146 KB), the WPA supplicant (77 KB), lwIP (51 KB), the radio layer, crypto and the shim
167	  (25 KB) in the flash; the driver's buffers, lwIP, the shim's task table and 24 KB of the heap (about 100 KB) in
168	  the RAM; the rest of the heap (248 KB) and lwIP's packet buffers (28 KB) in the pool. The heap, 272 KB, holds the
169	  WiFi library's own buffers (about 60 KB) and its tasks' stacks (4 to 8 KB each, by task, as a task starts: about
170	  6), and what is left is the app's (`malloc`; fm1-radio's HE-AAC player and HTTPS stream peak at 256 KB of it).
171	  That leaves an app about 170 KB of flash and a few KB of RAM.
172	  WiFi calibrates its radio at every start (a kept calibration was Bluetooth's, which the access point could not
173	  hear). `examples/wifi` is 420 KB of
174	  flash, 119 of 128 KB of RAM and 299 of 304 KB of pool; fm1-radio (MP3 and HE-AAC decoders, HTTPS) is
175	  576 KB, 127 KB and 300 KB.
176	- In a WiFi build, fm1-base's large font (the splash's name, the panel's screens) can go too:
177	  `#define APP_BIG_FONT FONT_M` in app.h saves 20 KB of flash.
178	- An app with fonts of its own can give them to fm1-base's screens (crash, safe mode, update, restore,
179	  calibration, the splash): `#define APP_SYS_TEXT` in app.h and its `app_sys_h`, `app_sys_w`, `app_sys_text`
180	  (`device/sys_text.c`); fm1-base's faces are then left out (LOOM-8: 18 KB).
181	
182	## Development over USB
183	
184	`tools/fm1_remote.py` drives an FM-1 running any fm1-base firmware as a player would: buttons, keys, encoders,
185	MASTER, and reads back what the screen says (the screen reader's channel), the last crash and the radio's log; with
186	WiFi, it turns it on and off, joins networks and reads its state (`wifi ...`).
187	For example, `tools/fm1_remote.py listen tap REC wait 3000 screen log`.
188	It finds the FM-1 as the web pages do (`tools/fm1ports.py`, the same rules as `web/fm1ports.js`): a port with an
189	FM-1's usual name, or else one that answers the screen reader's HELLO, whatever it is called; `--port NAME` picks one.
190	`tools/fm1_install.py`, `fm1_backup.py`, `fm1_mirror.py` and `fm1_debug.py` find it the same way.
191	
192	The site's installer page (`tools/make_site.py`, from `web/installer.html`) reads the same crash record and log in
193	Chrome or Edge: "Report a problem" shows them, ready to copy, so a player can send them without Python. The record
194	survives a restart, not switching off.
195	
196	The pages find the FM-1 with `web/fm1ports.js`, under any port name: a port with one of the FM-1's usual names, one
197	the player picked (Try), or one that answers the screen reader's HELLO, which every fm1-base firmware does. Only the
198	HELLO goes to other ports, three times: its ID, 7D, is the one for non-commercial use, which other gear ignores.
199	The [FM-1 Screen Reader](https://github.com/charlesvestal/fm1-reader)'s page uses the same file, as a copy.
200	
201	The screen reader's firmware side lives here too: `device/announce.c` and `tools/gen_words.py` (MPL-2.0, like the
202	rest; see LICENSING.md) are the one copy. fm1-reader keeps the page, the voice, the protocol (its PROTOCOL.md), the audit and the skill, and its
203	`tools/sync_announce.sh` copies these two files into the firmwares not on fm1-base.
204	
205	## .rfm1: your firmware in host apps
206	
207	An `.rfm1` file is your firmware built to run inside an app instead of on the FM-1: RemoteFM1 for iOS first, as
208	an instrument or an AUv3. It is the host simulator compiled to WebAssembly, the same app as on the FM-1, with a
209	manifest (name, version, licence, the source at its commit), your credits and the licence texts. Users download it
210	from your release and put it in the app's firmware folder. The format is RemoteFM1IOS's
211	[docs/RFM1-FORMAT.md](https://github.com/Quixotic7/RemoteFM1IOS/blob/main/docs/RFM1-FORMAT.md).
212	
213	    tools/build.py APP_DIR --rfm1                    # APP_DIR/build/rfm1/ID-dev+COMMIT.rfm1 (emcc, as --web)
214	    tools/build.py APP_DIR --rfm1 --release X.Y      # APP_DIR/build/NAME-X.Y.rfm1, beside NAME-X.Y.fwsc
215	
216	The ID is fm1.toml's `name` in lower case. Without `--release` the version is `dev+` and the app repository's commit.
217	The template's release workflow builds the release's `.rfm1` and attests it with the package.
218	The manifest's `source_url` is fm1.toml's `repo` at that commit, so commit (and push) what you build. Its `license`
219	is fm1.toml's `licence`, and its authors are `authors = ["..."]` or the repository's first author. The memory is fixed
220	at 8 MiB (`rfm1_memory_mib`, at most 32). The build checks the module against the format before it writes the file.
221	
222	In the app, the panel, screen, LEDs, sound, MIDI both ways, velocity and pressure (`APP_TOUCH`) and the screen
223	reader (over SysEx) work as in the browser emulator. Saved objects and the data area are kept by the app with its
224	state. There is no radio, no USB host and no environment (`getenv` returns nothing). `tests/rfm1_test.mjs FILE`
225	drives a file as a host app does.
226	
227	## firmware.json: your firmware in hubs
228	
229	Every build writes `firmware.json`, a description of the firmware for the places that list and install FM-1
230	firmwares (The Firmware Hub, RemoteFM1, M-Flasher): its name, author, licence, a paragraph on it, tags, the install
231	page, and the hardware it needs (the flash parts it saves to, the parts the build has, such as Bluetooth MIDI or USB
232	audio). It comes from fm1.toml (`author`, `description`, `tags`, `install`, `site`, with the site's `tagline`, `repo`,
233	`licence` and `credits`) and lands in `APP_DIR/build/` and, for an app in `app/`, at the repository's root, to commit.
234	The format, its fields and its vocabularies are in [docs/FIRMWARE-JSON.md](docs/FIRMWARE-JSON.md).
235	
236	## Moving a Felucca-based firmware here
237	
238	A Felucca-based firmware (GPL-3.0) can move onto fm1-base and felucca-bsp and keep its licence: their MPL-2.0 files
239	may be part of a GPL work, and stay MPL-2.0 file by file. It then has the platform's parts and fixes with every other
240	firmware, instead of its own copy of Felucca. `skill/felucca-to-fm1-base/` is a Claude skill that walks through the
241	move: the inventory (what is platform, what is the app), what fm1-base needs, the port, the checks (the app's
242	scenarios compared byte for byte with the old simulator's, then the FM-1), and the licensing files. It never changes
243	the firmware's licence: it asks. Relicensing to MPL-2.0 is needed only to link JieLi's Bluetooth or WiFi libraries;
244	`skill/felucca-to-fm1-base/RULES.md` has what it takes (`tools/provenance.py` finds Felucca's lines and whose they
245	are). To move a firmware with Claude Code, run this from inside its repository (Node.js's `npx` fetches the skill
246	into the project):
247	
248	    npx degit --force charlesvestal/fm1-base/skill/felucca-to-fm1-base .claude/skills/felucca-to-fm1-base && claude "Move this firmware onto fm1-base with the felucca-to-fm1-base skill"
249	
250	Claude starts with the inventory and shows it before changing anything. To have the skill in every project instead,
251	fetch it to `~/.claude/skills/felucca-to-fm1-base`. It reads as plain instructions too, without Claude.
252
```

2	
3	A base for M-VAVE FM-1 firmware, on felucca-bsp. A firmware is felucca-bsp (chip, board, update loader, packaging),
4	plus fm1-base (everything a firmware needs above the hardware), plus its own app. It is the platform layer that
5	FoMni-1, X0X, CTL-1 and the other firmwares share today, made into one maintained base.
6	
7	## Licence
8	
9	**Every file of fm1-base is MPL-2.0**, with a provenance that allows it:
10	
11	| Source | Why it may be MPL-2.0 |
12	| --- | --- |
13	| Leo Kuroshita's code from Felucca | his permission, recorded in hugelton/felucca-bsp#4; his name in `CREDITS.md` |
14	| Charles Vestal's code (the firmwares' platform layer: X0X, FoMni and the rest) | his own |
15	| keremimo's code | only what he has agreed to on the record (felucca-bsp#3; the second-core start once its PR has his comment; Melodee's code, 2026-10-31: LICENSING.md) |
16	
17	Nothing else goes in: no code by other Felucca contributors, no GPL code from anywhere. Every imported file's history
18	is checked first (its authors in git and, for files from Felucca, Felucca's README credits). Third-party material keeps its
19	own licence and is listed in `LICENSING.md`: the fonts (SIL OFL 1.1), JieLi's SDK files used by the build (Apache-2.0,
20	fetched, never committed).
21	
22	An app built on fm1-base may use any licence. MPL-2.0 applies file by file: changes to fm1-base's files are published
23	under MPL-2.0, the app's own files are the app's choice. A firmware that links JieLi's closed Bluetooth or Wi-Fi
24	libraries therefore has no GPL file in it at all.

26	## Layers
27	
28	```
29	app (ui.c, project.c, dsp/ ...)            the firmware's own code, any licence
30	  |  plat.h (the platform interface)
31	fm1-base  device: plat_fm1.c, main_fm1.c, panel.c, lcd.c, gfx.c, storage.c, midi_uart.c, announce.c
32	          host:   plat_host.c (simulator, scripted), web/emu (the simulator in the browser)
33	          tools:  build.py, fonts, words, installer and site pages
34	felucca-bsp (git submodule, pinned)  chip/ boards/fm1/ loader/ tools/fm1pkg.py tools/fm1_install.py
35	```
36	
37	The app sees only `plat.h`. The device and the host implement it, so every app runs, unchanged, on the FM-1, in the
38	host simulator (tests, screenshots) and in the browser.
39	
40	## The platform interface
41	
42	`plat.h` is the union of what the 13 firmwares use today (68 functions), in groups. A firmware turns on the optional
43	groups it needs, and only those are compiled in.
44	
45	| Group | Functions (today's names) | Used by |
46	| --- | --- | --- |
47	| core | `plat_ms`, `plat_buttons`, `plat_keys`, `plat_enc`, `plat_master`, `plat_leds`, `plat_glow`, `plat_play_red`, `plat_keys_dim`, `plat_store_load/save`, `plat_cpu_pct`, `plat_xruns` | all |
48	| MIDI | `plat_midi_in` (USB or TRS), `plat_midi_out`, `plat_midi3`, `plat_sysex`, `plat_midi_out_room`, `plat_midi_out_link`, `plat_midi_dropped`, SysEx in (`plat_sysex_get/done/send`) | all; the extras by some |
49	| storage extras | `plat_store_load_prev`, `plat_store_head`, raw sectors (`plat_gal_*`) | X0X, SPH-16, XY-1, Polly, Mocky |
50	| second core | `plat_cpu2_*`, `plat_core` (fm1.toml `cpu2 = true`; how to use it: [docs/SECOND-CORE.md](docs/SECOND-CORE.md)) | LOOM-8; X0X, NuSaw and SPH-16 on their own copies |
51	| analog keys | `plat_analog_*`, `plat_cap_probe`, `plat_sense` | Velo, MONK-1, CTL-1 |
52	| profiling | `plat_cycles*`, `plat_stalls*`, `plat_cpu_peak_pct`, `plat_irq_stack_*`, `plat_ticks24` | X0X, SPH-16, XY-1 |
53	| power | `plat_battery`, `plat_battery_raw`; the supply rails are fm1-base's own, set at boot, with no call ([docs/SECOND-CORE.md](docs/SECOND-CORE.md#the-supplies)) | X0X, SPH-16, NuSaw, LOOM-8 |
54	| crash | `plat_last_crash` | X0X, SPH-16, NuSaw, XY-1 |
55	| Bluetooth | `plat_ble_*` | CTL-1 |
56	| concurrency | `plat_lock`, `plat_unlock`, `plat_yield`, `plat_idle` | CTL-1, Mocky |
57	
58	The names stay as they are, so moving a firmware is a change of include paths, not of code. A firmware's own oddities
59	(X0X's sample slots) stay in that firmware.
60	
61	The app provides the other side: `app_init`, `app_frame` (the UI, about 60 a second), `app_render` (the audio,
62	called by the platform's audio interrupt), `app_tick` (1 kHz, optional), `app_say` (the screen reader), and
63	`app_config`: the block size, the second core, the USB names, the store's objects.
64	
65	## Build
66	
67	One `tools/build.py` for every firmware, driven by the firmware's `fm1.toml`: the name, the package identity
68	(`FM-1_` + digits), the USB names (felucca-bsp's `FELUCCA_USB_MANUFACTURER` / `FELUCCA_USB_PRODUCT`), the app's
69	sources, the optional groups, the fonts. It builds the app and the update loader, checks the rules (no `double`, no
70	hardware access outside the BSP and fm1-base's device files), and packs the `.fwsc` with felucca-bsp's `fm1pkg.py`.
71	`tools/run_tests.sh` builds the host simulator and runs the app's scripted tests. The web pages (installer, emulator,
72	backup) are generated from templates with the firmware's name and words file.
73	
74	The FM-1 tells its identity to the update handshake (felucca-bsp `chip/ota.c`, cmd 0x11). M-VAVE's M-UPGRADE 3.11
75	takes `NAME_` and one to three digits only, so the plain handshake gets the name, `_` and the first three digits
76	(`FM-1_11000100` -> `FM-1_110`); the handshake with the one-byte body 01 gets the whole identity. The installers
77	(`tools/fm1_install.py`, `web/fm1ota.js`, the backup page) ask that way when the plain answer is `NAME_` and three
78	digits, and keep the plain answer when nothing answers (M-VAVE's firmware, the loaders, older builds). The scheme is
79	PERF-1's (deamonSLINKY/PERF-1), so its tools and ours read each other's firmwares.
80	
81	## What fm1-base ships
82	
83	- `template/`: a minimal firmware to copy: a screen with text, the keys playing a sine voice, MASTER as the volume,
84	  USB-MIDI in and out, a saved setting, the screen reader. It builds, installs, updates and runs in the simulator.
85	- `examples/`: one small program per subject: the screen and fonts, keys and LEDs, audio, MIDI over USB and TRS,
86	  storage, the second core, and later Bluetooth MIDI.
87	- `docs/`: the interface, the build, porting a firmware, the licence.
88	
89	## Order of work
90	
91	1. The repository: felucca-bsp as a submodule; FoMni's platform layer, the host simulator, the web emulator and the
92	   tools brought in, each file checked for its authors, MPL-2.0 headers, `CREDITS.md`, `LICENSING.md`.
93	2. The template, flashed and tested on an FM-1: boot, screen, keys, audio, MIDI, save, reboot, update over USB. This is
94	   also the device test of felucca-bsp's latest changes (the supplies, the second core held on reset, the USB names).
95	3. hwtest gets an update path from the template's hooks; the real hwtest is run on a device; the second-core PR is tested.
96	4. CTL-1 moves onto fm1-base, with its Bluetooth build, which can then be released.
97	5. The other firmwares, one at a time; the optional groups come in with the first firmware that needs each.
98	6. After CTL-1's move: a skill, "move a Felucca fork onto felucca-bsp and fm1-base", written from what that move took.
99
````
</details></tool-use>

- **License:** The Open Textbook Library lists the conditions of use as the GNU Free Documentation License. MERLOT says the author permits copying, distribution, and modification under the GFDL terms.
- **Author and scope:** Robert Hutchinson of the University of Puget Sound wrote it. It is an openly licensed online, four-semester college music theory text, first published in 2017.
- **Content:** It runs from reading and writing pitches and rhythms through twelve-tone technique and minimalism. Its distinguishing focus is on melody and phrase analysis rather than mainly four-part SATB voice leading.
- **Reviews:** Reviewers on the Open Textbook Library praise its comprehensiveness and ancillary materials, but one suggests more examples from musical theatre and female composers.

Other sources in the results mention Creative Commons only for a different book, Catherine Schmidt-Jones's *Understanding Basic Music Theory*, which MERLOT says is CC BY.

22	 * at the start of the packed SRAM, as big as its one budget lets it), out of the way
23	 * of the XIP cache's misses: an audio path. It may call
24	 * only RAM code (other PLAT_RAM_CODE functions, felucca-bsp's RAM functions) and nothing through a pointer; the build
25	 * checks it over the disassembly, to any depth (tools/ramcode.py; fm1.toml ram_code_allow names the exceptions an app
26	 * vouches for). Not for code that runs with the flash off: it may read constants in the flash. XIP code it may not
27	 * call: the compiler's own calls (memcpy for a struct copy, a 64-bit divide), and a static inline helper the compiler
28	 * keeps out of line (at -Os it often does: fastmath.h's fm_exp2f), whose one copy is in XIP; a helper RAM code uses
29	 * is always_inline, or PLAT_RAM_CODE itself.
30	 * PLAT_FAR(fn): fn through a pointer the compiler cannot turn back into a direct call. RAM code and XIP code are
31	 * mostly farther apart than a direct call reaches (+-4 MiB), so XIP code calls RAM code this way (the linker refuses
32	 * a direct call that does not reach: "relocation truncated to fit"); a call from RAM code into XIP this way is one
33	 * the check refuses, unless allowed. The host: plain calls. */
34	#ifdef PLAT_HOST
35	#define PLAT_RAM_CODE
36	#define PLAT_FAR(fn) (&(fn))

Links: [{"title":"Interval recognition","url":"https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interval_recognition"},{"title":"Why interval drills alone don't make you hear music — and what does","url":"https://fifths-marketing.pages.dev/blog/functional-vs-interval-ear-training/"},{"title":"Musical intervals explained: what they are, how to recognize them, and what most apps get wrong","url":"https://fifths-marketing.pages.dev/blog/musical-intervals-explained/"},{"title":"public-pages-files-2025.frontiersin.org","url":"https://public-pages-files-2025.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2025.1723224/pdf"},{"title":"Interval recognition","url":"https://cavac.at/cavacopedia/Interval%20recognition"},{"title":"journals.ou.edu","url":"https://journals.ou.edu/jmtp/article/download/722/1563/1553"},{"title":"Interval recognition","url":"https://wikipedia.com/wiki/Interval_recognition"},{"title":"journals.ou.edu","url":"https://journals.ou.edu/jmtp/issue/download/74/72"},{"title":"How to Identify Intervals by Ear","url":"https://music-theory-practice.com/guides/how-to-identify-intervals-by-ear"},{"title":"• Skip to primary navigation","url":"https://www.stringkick.com/blog-lessons/interval-ear-training/"}]

The search turned up a fair amount of practitioner writing on this, but little direct experimental research comparing the two methods.

- **Reference songs:** Some teachers link each interval to the opening of a popular song, and those are called "reference songs". Wikipedia notes that others have shown that such familiar-melody associations are quite limited in scope, applicable only to the specific scale-degrees found in each melody. Another practitioner guide points out that almost all the famous reference songs give you ascending melodic intervals, not descending or harmonic ones.

- **Functional training:** Several blog-style sources argue that scale-degree training works better when built on a key. One says this is the functional ear training stage; it is the single highest-leverage step. They recommend that random pitches without tonal context come last, as a separate skill. Another source suggests that interval recognition is necessary — you need the raw discrimination — but it is not sufficient.

- **Research support is thin:** The claim that interval drilling doesn't transfer to musical hearing is mostly asserted in practitioner sources. One of them cites tonal-hierarchy work and on practitioner literature, without identifying specific studies. Another refers to "stacks of research" without citing any. The pedagogy-journal sources (Journal of Music Theory Pedagogy) appear only as titles or tables of contents, so I couldn't verify their findings. A 2025 Frontiers paper on absolute pitch and tonal context is relevant to how listeners use tonal cues, but it's about a different population and question.

- **Bottom line:** The consensus that tonal context helps is plausible and widely taught, but the search didn't surface a controlled study directly comparing functional and isolated interval training. Several of the most-cited sources are vendor blogs, so they should be treated as opinion. Searching for peer-reviewed aural-skills pedagogy studies, or the JMTP article "Interval and Scale-Degree Strategies in Melodic Perception," would be the next step for stronger evidence.

The One Note method is an ear training system by Bruce Arnold (published through Muse Eek Publishing) for developing relative pitch. The results describe it but don't explain its exercises in detail.

- **What it is:** One listing describes the book and audio CD as a new and exciting method of developing relative pitch ear training.
- **Levels:** The Complete edition bundles three levels, Beginning, Intermediate and Advanced. It is a compilation with 3 accompanying audio CDs. Each level is also sold separately.
- **Exercise format:** A blog post by Arnold describes one exercise as where you hear a cadence, note and then a pitch and then identify the pitch.
- **Progression:** Arnold suggests moving on once a student reaches roughly 50% correct on One Note, when he recommends starting "Direct Application Ear Training Volume One." Key note recognition comes after 80% correct on the Ear Training One Note Complete Advanced audio files.
- **Reception:** The publisher's site says the method is one of the best selling ear training systems, though that is the publisher's own claim. A vocal version is also available.

Caution: a Goodreads page describes the author as an English journalist and author who has lived in Ireland since 1957. That biography appears to be for a different person with the same name, so don't rely on it for the ear training author's background.

The search results suggest fsrs-rs itself is BSD-3-Clause, not MIT, though several FSRS implementations and bindings are MIT.

- **fsrs-rs license:** Two sources list the project's license as BSD-3-Clause. One is a metadata listing for the repository, and the other is its citation file, which names BSD-3-Clause as the license. The project's metadata lists the license as bsd-3-clause, and its CITATION.cff file also gives BSD-3-Clause. Your premise of an MIT license for fsrs-rs isn't supported by these results, so check the LICENSE file in the repo directly.
- **Rust and other ports:** The rs-fsrs crate is a separate Rust implementation, and its listing shows an MIT license. It also has official bindings for C/C++, Python, Java, and Node.js. The rs-fsrs repository is listed as MIT-licensed.
- **Embedding examples:** The R bindings (r-fsrs) wrap fsrs-rs and are MIT-licensed, with full FSRS-6 implementation via Rust bindings. A Dart/Flutter binding for fsrs-rs is also MIT, and it uses flutter_rust_bridge to embed the Rust core.
- **Other languages:** A Python package (fsrs on PyPI) is distributed under the MIT License. A pure TypeScript implementation is also MIT, and a Haskell port of FSRS-7 is MIT-licensed as well.
- **Algorithm background:** FSRS is designed to be used in Anki, and Anki 23.10 has already integrated FSRS as an alternative scheduler.

For embedding, the Rust crates are the most direct option if you need the optimizer and scheduler. If you need a permissive MIT dependency, rs-fsrs or one of the MIT-licensed bindings may be a better fit, but confirm each license before shipping.

214	static int st_read(uint32_t off, void *dst, uint32_t n)   /* 256-byte IRQ-off windows: audio keeps up */
215	{
216	    uint8_t *d = dst;
217	    while (n) {
218	        uint32_t k = n > 256u ? 256u : n, f = irq_save();
219	        int rc = FL_FAR(fl_read_ram)(off, d, k);
220	        irq_restore(f);
221	        if (rc)
222	            return rc;
223	        off += k;
224	        d += k;
225	        n -= k;
226	    }
227	    return 0;
228	}

/* SPDX-License-Identifier: MPL-2.0
 * Copyright (C) 2026 Charles Vestal */
/* The template: the smallest complete fm1-base firmware. Copy this directory to start a firmware.
 * This header is the app's half of the contract with the platform (device/unity.c, host/plat_host.c). */
#pragma once
#include <stdint.h>
#include "plat.h"

#define APP_NAME "TEMPLATE"
#define APP_SPLASH_RGB RGB(242, 120, 72)
#define APP_BLOCK 256u                   /* frames per audio block: 5.8 ms at 44.1 kHz */
#define APP_TOUCH                        /* velocity and pressure from the keys (lib/touch.h) */
#define APP_BTDEV                        /* Bluetooth MIDI devices (lib/btdev.h) */
#define APP_BLE_AT_BOOT (!template_ble_off())   /* Bluetooth at power-on: as the player left it (REC held) */
int template_ble_off(void);

/* the store: the app's objects, the panel calibration (the platform's) and Bluetooth's address and pairing among
 * them, and their flash offsets */
enum { OBJ_SETTINGS, OBJ_PANEL, OBJ_BLE, OBJ_NOBJ };
#define APP_STORE_MAP {0xFC000u, 0xDC000u, 0xDE000u}

/* the contract: the platform calls these */
void app_init(void);                     /* boot: the engine, then the saved settings (or defaults) */
void app_render(int32_t *lr, uint32_t n, uint32_t master_q12);   /* audio interrupt: n stereo frames, 24-bit */
void app_panic(void);                    /* silence now (before an update rewrites the flash) */
void app_ui_init(void);                  /* the first screen, after the splash */
void app_frame(void);                    /* the UI: input and a redraw, about 60 times a second */
void app_input_only(void);               /* between frames: input only */
void app_say(const char *a, const char *b);   /* a short message on the screen and to a screen reader */

/* the host simulator's checks (host/plat_host.c "expect"): octave, wave, note (-1 none), dirty, turnsN */
#define APP_HOST_EXPECT
int app_expect(const char *what, int *got);

"""Minimal LZ4 *block* format (no frame), written for the Felucca loader
wrapper: greedy hash-chain-free compressor and a decoder for self-checks.
Spec: https://github.com/lz4/lz4/blob/dev/doc/lz4_Block_format.md
(min match 4, last 5 bytes literals, last match starts >= 12 bytes before the end)."""


def _len_bytes(n):
    out = bytearray()
    while n >= 255:
        out.append(255)
        n -= 255
    out.append(n)
    return out


def compress(src: bytes) -> bytes:
    n, out, table = len(src), bytearray(), {}
    anchor, i = 0, 0
    limit = n - 12                                  # matches must start before this
    while i < limit:
        key = src[i:i + 4]
        cand = table.get(key)
        table[key] = i
        if cand is None or i - cand > 65535:
            i += 1
            continue
        mlen = 4                                    # extend; leave the last 5 bytes as literals
        while i + mlen < n - 5 and src[cand + mlen] == src[i + mlen]:
            mlen += 1
        lit = src[anchor:i]
        tok = (min(len(lit), 15) << 4) | min(mlen - 4, 15)
        out.append(tok)
        if len(lit) >= 15:
            out += _len_bytes(len(lit) - 15)
        out += lit
        off = i - cand
        out += bytes((off & 0xFF, off >> 8))
```
</details></tool-use>

The Open Music Theory chapter on popular music covers the doo-wop, singer/songwriter, and lament schemas, though the results don't include the full text of any one page.

- **Doo-wop:** The schema is I–vi–IV–V, and it is tied to 1960s pop. The doo-wop schema is I–vi–IV–V, and it was common in 1960s pop music. Its tonic is reached through fully authentic motion, as in classical music.
- **Singer/songwriter:** The common form is vi–IV–I–V, and the schema may be the best known of all the four-chord schemas. Its tonic is ambiguous because there is no authentic cadence.
- **Lament:** This is a classical-derived schema that descends from the tonic to the dominant. One source describes it as a four-chord schema that descends down the minor tetrachord from the tonic to the dominant. The name comes from early classical music, where the progression was used as the ground bass for songs of lament. Dire Straits' "Sultans of Swing" is given as a classic example of the lament in a pop/rock setting.

The chapter that covers these schemas is titled "Classical Schemas (in a Pop Context)," and it sits under the Popular Music unit. The doo-wop and singer/songwriter schemas are in the Four-Chord Schemas section, and the lament is in the classical-schemas section.

The search returned a Wikipedia article on the Nashville Number System, along with several guides and one academic article.

- **Basic idea:** The system swaps chord letters for scale-degree numbers, so the chords are described relative to the key. One guide notes it is primarily a practical notation for musical performance rather than harmonic analysis, which distinguishes it from Roman numeral analysis.
- **Chart layout:** Wikipedia says charts are usually laid out in four-measure lines, and several chords in one measure may be grouped with underlines (Charts are commonly arranged in lines of four measures, with each measure containing one or more numbers representing its chords.).
- **Key center:** The tonic has to be identified correctly, because it sets the reference point for every number (The chart's key center (tonic note) must be correctly determined to make the number system accurate. The tonic establishes the reference point from which all chord numbers are assigned.).
- **Transposition:** A North Carolina State University page says the system allows players to easily transpose songs into different keys. Its example in G is G-A-B-C-D-E-F#, with the chords numbered by scale position.
- **Major-key convention:** One guide points out that the chord symbols always reflect the major key. Another source says that for minor-key songs, the 1 chord is minor and charts usually note at the top whether the song is major or minor.
- **Rhythm and variation:** Rhythm is often left vague, so writers frequently add a specific rhythmic pattern (Rhythmic indications are often left vague in the Nashville number system). Notation also differs between charts, so one source warns that exact symbols vary slightly between players and charts.
- **Academic background:** Trevor de Clercq's 2019 article in the Journal of Music Theory Pedagogy describes the system as a notational practice used by commercial musicians and compares it with Roman numerals.

The Wikipedia "Chord chart" article also mentions the system, noting that musicians in Nashville use the Nashville Number System almost exclusively for conveying a song's structure and arrangement.

I didn't open the full pages, so these points come only from the search snippets.

The 2014 Macnamara meta-analysis and the related music studies gave different variance estimates for deliberate practice in music.

- **Macnamara, Hambrick & Oswald (2014, *Psychological Science*):** Across domains, deliberate practice accounted for 21% of the variance in music performance, against 26% for games and 18% for sports. The authors concluded that it matters, though less than its proponents had argued. Deliberate practice explained 26% of the variance in performance for games, 21% for music, 18% for sports, 4% for education, and less than 1% for professions.
- **Platz et al. (2014, *Frontiers in Psychology*):** This music-only meta-analysis of 13 studies found a higher figure. It found a correlation of 0.61 after correcting for unreliability. A 2018 review by Hambrick and colleagues says that corrected correlation implies that deliberate practice explained 37% of the variance.
- **Hambrick et al. (2014):** This earlier reanalysis of music and chess studies, which Platz et al. criticized, reported about 30% for music. One critique summarizes it as 34% and 30% of variance in chess and music performance, assuming a reliability of 0.80.
- **Later critique:** A 2021 paper in *Current Psychology* argues the meta-analyses underestimated deliberate practice's role, because many included measures did not assess individualized practice. The authors claim the explanatory power of deliberate practice has been considerably underestimated in the meta-analyses.

The main disagreement is about correcting for measurement reliability and about whether variance or correlation is the right metric. Macnamara et al. replied to Platz et al. that none of these criticisms challenge our conclusion that deliberate practice is not as important as Ericsson and colleagues have argued. The 2014 Macnamara figure of 21% is the unreliability-uncorrected cross-domain estimate, while the 30–37% figures are music-specific and corrected for measurement error.

        c ^= b << 8

            c = ((c << 1) ^ 0x1021) if c & 0x8000 else c << 1

def ldr_head(dcrc, a, b, attr, name):
    body = struct.pack("<HIIBBH16s", dcrc, a, b, attr, 0, 0, name)
    return struct.pack("<H", crc16(body)) + body


def ldr_wrap(image):
    """ota.bin = outer JLFS head (32 B) + inner head (32 B, load address) +
    blocks [clen u32][dlen u32][LZ4 block], dlen 4096 except the last"""
    blocks = bytearray()
    for i in range(0, len(image), 4096):
        raw = image[i:i + 4096]
        c = lz4blk.compress(raw)
        if len(c) > 4096 or lz4blk.decompress(c) != raw:
            raise SystemExit(f"loader: block {i // 4096} does not compress below 4096 B")
        blocks += struct.pack("<II", len(c), len(raw)) + c
    inner = ldr_head(crc16(image), len(image), LOADER_LOAD, 0, LOADER_NAME)
    body = inner + bytes(blocks)
    return ldr_head(crc16(body), 0x20, len(body), 0x41, LOADER_NAME) + body


def build_loader():
    LDR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    src = BSP / "loader"
    flags = [*CFLAGS, *inc(BSP / "chip", BSP / "boards" / "fm1")]
/* SPDX-License-Identifier: MPL-2.0 */
/* The resource region (fm1.toml resources = FILE, FM1B_RES): read-only data an app does not need to start (LOOM-8's
 * 909 samples), kept out of the image in sectors of the data area of the app's choosing (app.h APP_RES_BASE,
 * APP_RES_SECTORS) and read in place (plat_res). After Melodee's resource region (firmware/src/res.c, by Kerem Kilic,
 * Ellic Studio; used under MPL-2.0 with permission): the build knows its payload's length and CRC-32 (build.py writes
 * fm1_res.h from the file), so a firmware finds whether the region holds its own. The package carries it and the
 * update loader writes it after the app (felucca-bsp loader/ldr_core.c ldr_res, as Melodee's), from any host; the host
 * can also write it itself (tools/fm1_resources.py, fm1_install.py, the installer page: RES_REQ below), and an update
 * that keeps the payload keeps the region.
 * Missing, torn or another build's: plat_res 0, and the app does without (its own words for it).
 *
 * The transfer is the restore's (backup.c): the host's RES_REQ (length, CRC-32), then the device pulls the payload
 * with read requests (ota_read; addresses are the payload's offsets) and reports by reading RS_OK_ADDR or
 * RS_FAIL_ADDR | code. The device checks the request against its build first, so nothing is erased for another
 * build's file; one that holds it already answers at once.
 *   APP_RES_BASE        header: magic, length, CRC-32 of the payload, header CRC (written last: the commit record)
 *   APP_RES_BASE + 32   the payload, read in place through the unencrypted window (plat_data)
 * A pooled store whose move from the A/B pairs has not finished (storage.c st_pool_boot) may still have projects in
 * the region's sectors: no write until it has. */
#define RES_REQ 0x44u                               /* the host's request (ota.c framing; backup.c's are 0x41..0x43) */
#define RES_HEAD 32u
#define RES_MAGIC 0x31534552u                       /* "RES1" */
#define RES_E_BUILD 20                              /* another build's resources */
#define RES_E_STORE 21                              /* the store's move into its pool not done (the next boot: again) */
#define RES_E_CHECK 22                              /* the payload as written does not check */
typedef struct { uint32_t magic, len, crc, rsv[4], hcrc; } res_hdr_t;
_Static_assert(sizeof(res_hdr_t) == RES_HEAD, "the resource commit record");

- **The change:** Creative Commons announced in June 2023 that Wikipedia and other Wikimedia projects have now adopted version 4.0 of the Creative Commons BY-SA license. It was implemented through a revision to the project's Terms of Use, and the Wikimedia Foundation's own post describes it as part of a recent Terms of Use (ToU) update.
- **Why:** Creative Commons says the move lets Wikipedia incorporate content from a variety of useful sources that also use CC 4.0 licenses, including publications from the United Nations and many national governments. The Foundation says the 4.0 version is more accessible, globally compatible, simplified, and readable.
- **Conflicting sources:** Several pages still describe the older setup. A Meta-Wiki page says almost all content of almost all Wikimedia projects is dual-licensed under CC BY-SA 3.0 and GFDL, and a dumps license page says the Terms of Use are controlling. Those pages look outdated, and the Meta page is explicitly just one person's research and not official documentation. The Wikipedia reuse and copyright pages in the results mention CC BY-SA 3.0 or unversioned references, so they may predate the change.
- **Current Wikipedia template:** Wikipedia's attribution notice template includes a CC BY-SA 4.0 option, which suggests the 4.0 license is in active use.

I did not verify whether text added before the change remains under 3.0 or was relicensed. The Terms of Use page itself would be the authoritative source for that.

The search turned up several copies and mirrors of the English Wikipedia article on the Andalusian cadence, plus some non-Wikipedia reference sites. The mirrors differ somewhat, so check the live Wikipedia page for exact wording.

- **Notation:** The progression is written i–VII–VI–V for minor keys. In Phrygian terms it is iv–III–II–I, or i–♭VII–♭VI–V in Aeolian terms ([iv–III–II–I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_numeral_analysis) progression with respect to the [Phrygian mode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phrygian_mode) or i–♭VII–♭VI–V progression with respect to the [Aeolian). One mirror gives the same descent for natural or melodic minor and notes a harmonic-minor variant, i–♭VII–VI–V (i – VII – VI – V with respect to a natural or melodic minor key, the two being identical in descent).
- **Character:** A reference site describes the bass as descending stepwise from the minor tonic to the dominant, with a tense VI–V semitone that carries Phrygian cadential motion (In i – VII – VI – V, the bass descends stepwise from minor tonic to dominant. The VI – V semitone forms a Phrygian cadential motion and approaches V with particular intensity.).
- **Genre:** It is associated with flamenco and also appears in rock. One mirror cites "Runaway" by Del Shannon as a rock example (It is heard in rock songs such as "Runaway" by Del Shannon.).
- **Origins:** The triad-based form is generally dated to the Renaissance or later. One mirror says it may not have occurred earlier than the Renaissance, though the use of parallel thirds or sixths was evident as early as the 13th century.
- **Relation to Passamezzo antico:** One mirror notes that the progression resembles the first four measures of the 15th century Passamezzo antico; i – ♭VII – i – V.
- **Usage:** One mirror says it is most often used as an ostinato (repeating over and over again).

1	# 接口與連線
2	
3	## 各接口能做什麼
4	
5	| 接口 | 能做 | 不能做 |
6	|---|---|---|
7	| **USB-C** | 充電、USB MIDI in/out、韌體更新、USB audio（依韌體）、自訂 HID 裝置（依韌體）、USB host（只有少數韌體，見下） | 供電給接上的裝置 |
8	| **3.5 mm TRS MIDI IN** | 接收其他設備的 note、CC、clock | 不是 MIDI OUT |
9	| **3.5 mm 音訊輸出** | 立體聲類比輸出到耳機、mixer、錄音介面 | 不是 audio in，也不是 MIDI |
10	| **Bluetooth MIDI** | 硬體本身有無線電（SoC 內建 Bluetooth 與 WiFi）。原廠、CTL-1、Melodee、RemoteFM1、ChoralRoot 會用 | 要韌體開啟才有。SLOOP 不支援，它不開無線電。Agent Deck 也不支援：它的基底 Dinghy 完全沒有藍牙程式 `[上游]` |
11	
12	## 沒有音訊輸入：能不能當 sampler { #no-audio-in }
13	
14	FM-1 **沒有任何類比音訊輸入**，沒有麥克風，3.5 mm 孔只是輸出。所以不能像一般 sampler 那樣把線接進來錄。`[上游]`
15	
16	聲音要進到 FM-1，只能**從電腦或手機用數位方式送進去**，而且要韌體支援：
17	
18	| 方式 | 例子 | 狀態 |
19	|---|---|---|
20	| 從網頁上傳 sample 檔案 | SLOOP 的 [Web Editor](../firmware/sloop/web-editor.md)（4 個 slot，可以丟長錄音進去 CHOP）、官方 Workbench、Mini-Grain、ECHOFIELD 的 companion web app | `[上游]` |
21	| 讓 FM-1 當 USB 音效卡的**輸出端**，收主機播的聲音 | CTL-1（iPad 的聲音會從 FM-1 播出來，我實測過）、FM1 Audio Router | `[實機]` CTL-1 |
22	| 收主機的 USB 音訊並錄成 sample | ECHOFIELD 的說明寫 "your own samples (or recorded over USB)"，但沒說是哪個方向 | 沒查證 `[調研]` |
23	
24	所以「手機或網頁 + FM-1」的組合可以做到 sampler 的效果：在手機或電腦上錄好、剪好，再上傳到支援 sample 的韌體。ChoralRoot 做不到，它的聲音全是合成的，沒有 sample 引擎（GRAIN 引擎是對它自己生成的素材做 granular，不能載入外部 sample），USB 音訊也只有輸出到主機的方向。`[上游]` `[實機]`
25	
26	Firmware Hub 上找 sampler 類韌體：在 [catalog](https://thefirmwarehub.com/) 搜尋 sample、granular。
27	
28	## USB-C：device，不是 host
29	
30	FM-1 是 USB device。USB 鍵盤直接插在 FM-1 上不會動，因為兩邊都是 device，中間需要一個 host：電腦、手機或 USB MIDI host box。
31	
32	**例外（更正 2026-11-17）**：ChoralRoot 0.31 起有 **Options → USB Host**，打開後 USB-C 變成 USB MIDI host，可以直接接一台 USB MIDI 鍵盤，或用一條 USB-C 線把兩台 FM-1 互接。限制：FM-1 不供電，鍵盤要透過有供電的 hub 或 OTG 轉接頭；只支援 full-speed；開著時電腦、USB audio、更新都不能用；每次開機都回到一般 device 模式，不會存。`[上游]`（[release notes](https://github.com/Quixotic7/ChoralRootFM1/blob/main/docs/releases/0.31.md)）其他韌體預設仍是 device。
33	
34	反過來，電腦對 FM-1 可以做的事很多：
35	
36	- 接收琴鍵與旋鈕送出的 MIDI note / CC。
37	- 送 MIDI 回去控制合成器或 sequencer。
38	- 用支援 USB audio 的韌體直接數位錄音。
39	- 透過雙向 MIDI / SysEx 自訂螢幕內容、LED 狀態與 host 控制協定（Agent Deck 就是這樣做的）。
40	- 用自訂韌體讓 FM-1 變成 HID 鍵盤 / 滑鼠（Trireme）。
41	
42	注意不同韌體的 MIDI mapping 不同。不能假設每個實體按鍵在原廠韌體下都會送出獨立事件。`[調研]`
43	
44	## 兩台 FM-1 互連 { #two-units }
45	
46	有沒有辦法讓兩台 FM-1 直接互傳？硬體和 fm1-base 都留了路，但 2026-11-17 為止沒有找到有人在兩台實機上做過的紀錄。`[上游]` `[調研]`
47	
48	| 方式 | 怎麼接 | 限制 | 狀態 |
49	|---|---|---|---|
50	| **藍牙直連** | 一台開 `ble_central = true` 去掃描、連上另一台（它以 `FM-1 XXXX` 廣播 BLE MIDI） | fm1-base 自己的 BLE stack（`ble_stack = "own"`）一次只能有一條藍牙 MIDI 連線，連著另一台時電腦就不能走藍牙（USB 還可以）；JieLi 的 stack 可以兩條同時連，但會丟掉收到的 SysEx。central 的 connection interval 是 11.25 ms | fm1-base 只在模擬的無線電上測過（`docs/bt/BLE-DEVICES-DESIGN.md`、`tests/bt/ble_f2f_test.c`），沒有在兩台實機上測過 `[上游]` |
51	| **USB-C 線** | 一台切成 USB host（fm1-base `usb_host = true`，或 ChoralRoot 的 Options → USB Host） | FM-1 的 USB 口不供電；兩台都有電池，所以被接的那台可能不需要，但 FM-1 在沒有 VBUS 時會不會被列舉，沒有文件。fm1-base 的 host 模式收不到 SysEx，也不送 SysEx，note 和 CC 可以；它的 host 輸出路徑還沒在實機驗證 | ChoralRoot 0.31 的 release notes 說可以用 USB-C 線把兩台互接；[MIDIMON](https://github.com/ignis32/midimonitor_fm1) 的作者說接的裝置要有自己的電源（「例如另一台 FM-1」），並用它 debug 另一台 `[上游]` |
52	| **經過電腦** | 兩台都接電腦（USB 或藍牙），由電腦轉送；也可以經網路，例如 Vail | 要有電腦 | 最可靠 |
53	| TRS MIDI | — | FM-1 只有 MIDI IN，沒有 OUT，做不到雙向 | 不可行 |
54	
55	要讓同一個程式走得過以上每一條路，最穩的是只用 note on / off 這類一般 MIDI 訊息，不要依賴 SysEx。自製的[摩斯電碼機](../dev/morse.md)就是這樣設計：線上只傳按鍵的按下與放開。
56	
57	## TRS MIDI IN
58	
59	需要 **TRS-to-DIN MIDI 轉接線**。沒聲音時試另一種型式（Type A / Type B）。
60	
61	SLOOP 下的 channel 對應：
62	
63	| MIDI channel | 播放 |
64	|---|---|
65	| 1、2、3 | synth track 1、2、3 |
66	| 10 | drum track |
67	| 其他 | 目前選取的 track |
68	
69	可以在 GLO → MIDI 改。MIDI clock in 可從 USB 或 TRS 進來（GLO → SYSTEM → SYNC）。
70	
71	## USB audio（SLOOP）
72	
73	SLOOP 下 FM-1 同時是一個名為 **"Felucca"** 的 USB audio 輸入：44.1 或 48 kHz、16-bit stereo、class compliant，不需要 driver。錄到的是 master 輸出，跟耳機聽到的一樣。MIDI、Web Editor、installer 都走同一條線。
74	
75	- 音量：按住 `HOME` 進選單 → **USB AUDIO**。`MASTER` 跟著 master 旋鈕；`FULL` 是固定滿音量，適合沒有輸入增益的錄音介面。
76	- 安裝後第一次要拔插一次，電腦才會重新辨識成 MIDI + audio 裝置。
77	
78	## 用電腦接收 MIDI 的最小範例
79	
80	確認電腦看到的 MIDI port（需要 `pip install mido python-rtmidi`）：
81	
82	```python
83	import mido
84	
85	print(mido.get_input_names())
86	with mido.open_input(mido.get_input_names()[0]) as port:
87	    for msg in port:
88	        print(msg)
89	```
90	
91	這是通用的 `mido` 用法，不是某個上游專案的指令。port 名稱依韌體而定。
92
````

````text
1	# Flash 配置圖
2	
3	FM-1 的 flash 是 1 MiB，分成 256 個 4 KiB 的 sector。誰把什麼放在哪裡，決定了換韌體時什麼會留下、什麼會被蓋掉。這頁把各個來源的說法和我自己備份的比對放在一起。
4	
5	## 總覽
6	
7	| 位址 | 內容 | 來源 |
8	|---|---|---|
9	| `0x00000`–`0x03FFF` | **boot head**：bootloader 與 boot 設定（16 KiB）。壞了就開不了機 | `[上游]` M-Flasher、Unbricker |
10	| `0x04000`–`0x92FFF` | **韌體區**。多數韌體（原廠 V15、SLOOP、Agent Deck、CTL-1）佔這段 | `[實機]` M-Flasher 的寫入計畫 |
11	| `0x93000`–`0xE8FFF` | 原廠 V15 的**設定區**。社群韌體也把資料放在這裡面 | `[上游]` |
12	| `0xE9000` | Bluetooth 資料（配對） | `[上游]` |
13	| `0xEA000`–`0xFBFFF` | 原廠音色（factory voices） | `[上游]` |
14	| `0xFC000`–`0xFEFFF` | M-Flasher 的圖上標為 free；Felucca 系拿來放全域設定 | `[實機]` |
15	| `0xFF000`–`0xFFFFF` | key / MAC，裝置自己的資料 | `[上游]` |
16	
17	M-Flasher 的 flash map 用顏色標的就是這些：BOOT `00–03`、FIRMWARE `04–92`、SETTINGS `93–E8`、PAIRINGS `E9`、SOUNDS `EA–FB`、free `FC–FE`、MAC `FF`。
18	
19	## 韌體區不一定只到 `0x92FFF`
20	
21	| 韌體 | 佔用範圍 | 來源 |
22	|---|---|---|
23	| SLOOP 2.8.5、Agent Deck 0.7、CTL-1 1.0.3 | `0x04000`–`0x92FFF`（實際寫入到 `0x8FFFF`） | `[實機]` |
24	| Conductor 0.1（自製，fm1-base） | `0x04000`–`0x92FFF`（實際寫入 `0x04000`–`0x8EFFF`、`0x91000`–`0x91FFF`） | `[實機]` M-Flasher 的計畫：140 sectors |
25	| Morse 0.1 / 0.2（自製，fm1-base） | `0x04000`–`0x92FFF`（實際寫入：Conductor 0.3 → 0.1 是 `0x04000`–`0x21FFF`，0.1 → 0.2 是 `0x04000`–`0x23FFF`） | `[實機]` M-Flasher 的計畫：30、32 sectors |
26	| **ChoralRoot 0.41** | `0x04000`–**`0x9EFFF`** | `[實機]` M-Flasher 的計畫：152 sectors |
27	| **原廠 V16** | 到 **`0xA8FFF`** | `[上游]` Unbricker |
28	
29	超出 `0x92FFF` 的韌體會直接蓋掉別人放在 `0x93000` 之後的資料。
30	
31	## Felucca 系韌體的資料位置
32	
33	Felucca、SLOOP、ChoralRoot 以及 Dinghy、fm1-base 系的韌體大多沿用同一套位址 `[上游]`：
34	
35	| 位址 | 內容 |
36	|---|---|
37	| `0x97000` 起 | project（曲子） |
38	| `0x9F000` | SLOOP 的 autosave（和 ChoralRoot 的 FM6 bank 是同一個物件編號） |
39	| `0xA0000` 起 | samples |
40	| `0xDA000`–`0xDBFFF` | 自製 [Morse](../dev/morse.md#flash) 的設定與學習進度（這台機器的備份裡這兩個 sector 都是空的） |
41	| `0xDC000` 起 | user preset bank；CTL-1 與 fm1-base 的 app（含 Conductor）用來放面板校正 |
42	| `0xDE000` | CTL-1 的 Bluetooth 設定 |
43	| `0xE0000` | 更新時暫存 update loader |
44	| `0xF2000`–`0xF3FFF` | RemoteFM1 第一次開 Bluetooth 時寫入 |
45	| `0xFC000` | 全域設定。**SLOOP、Agent Deck、CTL-1 都寫這裡** |
46	| `0xFE000` | SLOOP autosave 的另一份 |
47	
48	因為位址共用，韌體之間會互相踩到對方的資料，也會讀到對方留下的東西。
49	
50	## 我的機器上實際發生的 `[實機]`
51	
52	用各階段的完整備份逐 sector 比對：
53	
54	| 動作 | 改變的 sector |
55	|---|---|
56	| 原廠 015 → 裝 SLOOP 並玩過 | 韌體區，加上 `0x97000`、`0x9F000`、`0xFC000`、`0xFD000`、`0xFE000` |
57	| → Agent Deck | 韌體區，加上 `0xFC000`（蓋掉 SLOOP 的設定） |
58	| → 回 SLOOP | 韌體區，加上 `0xFE000`。曲子還在 |
59	| → CTL-1 | 韌體區，加上 `0xDE000`、`0xDF000`、`0xFC000`、`0xFD000` |
60	| → ChoralRoot | `0x04000`–`0x9EFFF`，蓋掉了 `0x97000` 的 SLOOP project（已執行，尚未用備份比對確認其他 sector） |
61	| → Conductor | 韌體區 140 個 sector（`0x04000`–`0x8EFFF`、`0x91000`–`0x91FFF`）。開機後不寫任何資料（預演 `[模擬]`；實機尚未用備份比對） |
62	
63	原廠出廠時 `0x93000`、`0xE9000`–`0xF2000`、`0xFA000`、`0xFB000` 有資料，`0xFC000`–`0xFE000` 是空的。
64	
65	## 自己比對兩份備份
66	
67	```python
68	S = 4096
69	a = open("backups/A/x.bin", "rb").read()
70	b = open("backups/B/y.bin", "rb").read()
71	print([hex(i * S) for i in range(256) if a[i * S:(i + 1) * S] != b[i * S:(i + 1) * S]])
72	```
73	
74	## 這對操作的意義
75	
76	- **只重裝韌體會保留資料區**，所以 SLOOP ↔ Agent Deck 來回曲子還在。
77	- **韌體比較大的（ChoralRoot、V16）會吃掉資料區**，回去時要還原備份。
78	- **共用的 `0xFC000` 每換一次就被蓋一次**，各韌體的全域設定不會跨韌體保留。
79	- **原廠音色在 `0xEA000`–`0xFBFFF`**，有些韌體會寫這一段。只有原廠備份救得回來。
80	- 更完整的後果見[變磚的原理與分級](../getting-started/bricking.md)與[多韌體切換](../firmware/switching.md)。
81
````

The search turned up research on scale-degree versus interval strategies in melodic dictation, though little that directly tests Karpinski's own claims.

- **Strategy comparison:** William Lake's article on interval and scale-degree strategies says that neither approach is ideal for all situations. It identifies scale-degree thinking as best suited to tonal melodies (a scale-degree strategy is most suitable for tonal melodies), and notes that it helps a listener recover quickly after a misjudged leap (4-8). Lake also describes a flexible strategy that switches between intervals and scale degrees as the melody demands (4-9). The article traces back to W. Jay Dowling's 1986 study of scale-degree versus interval representation (4-2).
- **Interval difficulty:** A University of Tennessee master's thesis reports that students that have the most difficulty in melodic dictation usually have difficulty in interval identification.
- **Karpinski's framework:** Karpinski's 2000 book *Aural Skills Acquisition* has a full chapter on melodic dictation, and a 1990 paper by him is cited for a model of melodic dictation stages (10-2). Karpinski advocates a "proto-notation" method using solmization for dictation (1-5), and a reviewer notes that he argues it is quicker and less troublesome for students than standard melodic notation.
- **Recent commentary:** A 2021 *Music Theory Online* response by Elizabeth West Marvin discusses Karpinski's treatment of tonic inference and says his account of scale-degree perception draws on listener ratings but not on transitional-probability evidence (1-1, 1-9).

I found no direct experimental comparison of scale-degree and interval dictation accuracy that uses Karpinski's method. The Lake and Dowling material is the closest match to the question.

# FM-1 panel and audio contracts

Both drivers are header implementations. Include them in one translation unit,
like the other board headers, with `-Ichip -Iboards/fm1`. Initialize TIMER4 with
`fm1_time_init()` before either driver's startup delays. Applications serialize
access to each peripheral; neither driver supplies locks or a scheduler.

## Panel: `boards/fm1/fm1_lcd.h`

`fm1_lcd_init()` configures the SPI pins and the FM-1's ST7789 panel, waits for
reset and sleep-out, and selects RGB565, RGB colour order, IPS inversion and a
240 by 240 top-left coordinate space. The default SPI divider is 4. Its clock is
LSB / 5, so applications that change the system clock must account for that.
The original `fm1_lcd_hw.h` transport remains available for existing users.

- `fm1_lcd_fill_rect(x, y, w, h, rgb)` fills a rectangle with a native RGB565 value:
  red is `0xF800`, green `0x07E0`, blue `0x001F`.
- `fm1_lcd_blit(x, y, w, h, pixels, pixel_count)` sends contiguous row-major
  `uint16_t` RGB565 pixels. `pixel_count` is the available source element count,
  at least `w * h`. No stride, clipping, scaling or colour conversion is implicit.
- Zero width or height succeeds without touching hardware or reading pixels.
  Nonempty rectangles must fit completely inside the display. Overflowing
  coordinates, out-of-bounds rectangles, null pixel pointers and short sources
  return `-2` before a transfer starts.
- Both calls block until completion. They stage one row in a 480-byte static
  buffer (a header static: one per translation unit that includes `fm1_lcd.h`), sending the high byte first. The source may be in RAM or XIP and may be
  reused when the call returns. Normal C pointer validity/alignment and the
  supplied source capacity are the caller's responsibility.
- `0` means success. A transport timeout returns `-1`, increments the existing
  `fm1_lcd_timeouts`, releases CS and switches SPI1 off (`fm1_lcd_spi_off()`).
  Reinitialize before retrying; the panel may contain a partial rectangle.
  `fm1_lcd_wait()` in the low-level transport now returns this status too, but
  leaves SPI1 on: existing callers that initialize once and ignore the result
  (fm1-base's `device/lcd.c`, `loader/ldr_screen.c`) keep drawing after a
  timeout, as before.

Calls share staging RAM and SPI1. Do not call from nested interrupts or another
core while a transfer is active, or mix raw transport calls with panel operations
without the same serialization. The driver initializes the backlight on, as the
original transport did. `fm1_lcd_backlight(on)` still controls it; applications
using TIMER5 key scanning must protect this shared port-A read/modify/write
against that ISR, as documented in `fm1_lcd_hw.h`.

## Audio: `boards/fm1/fm1_audio.h`

### Fixed sample format and clock

Every frame is two `int32_t` words in left, right order. Samples are signed Q23:
`-8388608` through `8388607`, sign-extended into the 32-bit container, with zero
for silence. The significant bits occupy bits 23:0, **not** bits 31:8. For
example, positive full scale is `0x007FFFFF`, negative full scale is `0xFF800000`.
A signed PCM16 sample becomes this format by multiplying by 256. Clip before
storing; the driver does not saturate, convert float/PCM16, or resample.

The supported request is `FM1_AUDIO_RATE` (44100), the **nominal** 44.1 kHz family.
On the recognized stock audio PLL configuration, the hardware frame period is
544 ticks of the 24 MHz reference: `FM1_AUDIO_RATE_NUM / FM1_AUDIO_RATE_DEN`, or
about **44,117.647 Hz**, roughly +400 ppm relative to exact 44,100. Reference
oscillator tolerance applies too. A 256-frame half lasts about 5.803 ms.
Use this physical ratio for deadline calculations; nominal 44100 is appropriate

The results are mostly jazz-oriented, and none directly cover a pop root-fifth-octave pattern.

- **Core shell idea:** Shell voicings are a left-hand technique built from the root plus the 3rd and 7th, and they are the usual choice when the melody is busy. They are most commonly played using R-7 or R-3-7 of the chord voiced exclusively in our left hand.
- **Why use them:** Shells free the right hand for embellishments. They 'free up' our right hand for additional melodic embellishments such as turns and grace notes.
- **Beginner-friendly:** One lesson describes shells as simple but will give a lot more clean and polished sound than using just root position chords.
- **Alternating patterns:** One source suggests mixing shells with arpeggios to add movement. Alternating shell voicings and left hand arpeggios creates more interest and movement in the left hand.
- **Pop relevance:** Lead-sheet courses on Over the Rainbow and Summertime at beginner level teach the right hand melody, left hand shells, and a few easy tricks. Those are jazz standards rather than pop songs.

I found no source describing a root–fifth–octave pop pattern, so that part of your query is unconfirmed by these results. Searching for "pop piano root fifth octave pattern" or "pop piano left hand octaves" would likely fill that gap.
